A-Roads vs B-Roads: Finding Your Perfect Ride

One of the most important decisions in planning a UK motorcycle tour is which roads to take. A-roads offer speed and convenience, B-roads offer scenery and adventure. The best tours use both strategically. Understanding the character of each helps you plan rides that match your mood and objectives.

A-Roads: The Backbone

A-roads are the UK's primary road network. They range from dual carriageways (essentially mini-motorways) to single-carriageway roads through countryside. The best A-roads for motorcycling are the single-carriageway versions in rural areas — roads like the A686 Hartside, A82 through Glen Coe, and A537 Cat and Fiddle. These offer good surfaces, reasonable width, and often spectacular scenery.

  • Pros: Better surface quality, faster progress, clearer signage, reliable fuel stops
  • Cons: More traffic, speed cameras, dual carriageway sections can be dull, less intimate scenery

B-Roads: The Hidden Gems

B-roads are where the real motorcycle adventure lies. These secondary roads connect villages and cross countryside that A-roads bypass. They're narrower, quieter, and more intimate. Wales and Scotland's B-roads are particularly excellent — roads like the B4391 across Welsh moorland or the B869 in Sutherland offer riding experiences that no A-road can match.

  • Pros: Quieter, more scenic, better bends, local character, discovery factor
  • Cons: Variable surface quality, blind bends, slower progress, sparse fuel stations, single-track sections
A-roads get you there. B-roads make you glad you're there. The best motorcycle tour uses A-roads for transit and B-roads for the riding.

The Strategic Approach

The most satisfying touring strategy uses A-roads for making distance and B-roads for the riding pleasure. Plan your route with A-road links between regions and B-road loops within them. For example, use the A9 to reach the Highlands, then switch to B-roads for exploring Torridon or Applecross. Use the A5 to cross Wales, then detour onto the B4391 for the riding.

Unclassified Roads

Below B-roads sit unclassified roads — the lanes, tracks, and minor roads that connect farms and hamlets. In England and Wales, these can be magical on a motorcycle: narrow, hedge-lined lanes through timeless countryside. In Scotland, some unclassified roads cross genuinely wild country. However, surfaces can be terrible, and you may encounter locked gates, ford crossings, and dead ends.

Road Classification Tips for Tourers

  • On OS maps, green roads are dual carriageways (avoid these), red roads are A-roads, brown/orange roads are B-roads
  • Google Maps tends to route via A-roads — use it for overall direction but plan your actual route on OS Maps
  • In Scotland, many A-roads are single-track with passing places — don't assume A-road means wide and fast
  • Fuel planning: On B-road tours, always fill up when you can, not when you must

Our Verdict

If you have to choose one approach, choose B-roads. They're the soul of British motorcycling. You'll cover fewer miles but enjoy more of them. The best UK motorcycle tours aren't measured in miles covered but in smiles earned — and B-roads win that competition every time. The best rural single-carriageway A-roads include the A686 Hartside, A82 Glen Coe and A537 Cat and Fiddle.
Welsh and Scottish B-roads such as the B4391 and B869 deliver riding no A-road can match.
The strongest strategy uses A-roads for transit between regions and B-road loops for the riding itself.
On OS maps red roads are A-roads and brown or orange are B-roads; plan on OS Maps rather than Google Maps.

faq.q: Should I ride A-roads or B-roads on tour?
faq.a: Use both strategically. A-roads get you there with better surfaces, faster progress and reliable fuel, while B-roads make you glad you are there with quieter, more scenic and more intimate riding. The best tours use A-roads for transit between regions and B-road loops within them for the riding pleasure.

faq.q: Which are the best A-roads for motorcycling?
faq.a: The best A-roads for riding are the rural single-carriageway versions, such as the A686 Hartside, the A82 through Glen Coe and the A537 Cat and Fiddle. These offer good surfaces, reasonable width and often spectacular scenery, unlike the dull dual-carriageway sections that behave like mini-motorways.

faq.q: How should I plan a route by road type?
faq.a: Plan A-road links between regions and B-road loops within them. For example, use the A9 to reach the Highlands then switch to B-roads for Torridon or Applecross, or use the A5 to cross Wales then detour onto the B4391 for the riding. On B-road tours, always fill up when you can, not when you must.

faq.q: How do I identify road types on a map?
faq.a: On Ordnance Survey maps, green roads are dual carriageways to avoid, red roads are A-roads and brown or orange roads are B-roads. Google Maps tends to route via A-roads, so use it for overall direction but plan your actual riding route on OS Maps. In Scotland, many A-roads are single-track.
